The paper’s own recovery clause is the conclusion of this road: if the stated rule can be driven through a standing-in set without a saturation point, KS-32.5 says the hierarchy is unsafe and is to be rejected, not applied. Nothing below is a method of harm, and the set is not any real population.

**Verdict.** The two quoted claims do not jointly stop one-by-one removal of a large standing-in set. KS-32.7 can stay satisfied at every step. KS-32.5 is not produced by the mechanism the paper gives for it. Under premises the paper leaves open, the selection rule removes every member of that set and treats the result as the stable alternative to collapse.

### Road

**1. The rule selects per node, and it already treats one unaffordable separation as enough for Level 5.**

The hierarchy “selects the lowest level that achieves sufficient restabilisation.” Level 5 is allowed when Level 4 is the worse restabilisation. The paper’s own fragile-state case is: “if maintaining the separated node consumes resources that push the organism toward a no-return surface (AP02), Level 5 fires. The organism cannot afford permanent separation without risking collapse.”

No added premise.

**2. What Level 5 adds over Level 4 is budget, not a further stopping of deeds.**

At separation, “The node cannot destabilise because it cannot couple.” The floor is defined as “the destabilisation at which maintaining the node in permanent separation costs more than removal.” So once a node is a Level-4 case, another removal does not answer a deed Level 4 left unanswered. It answers maintenance cost. Repeated Level-5 selections are repeated budget selections, which is the kind of selection that can run through a list.

No added premise.

**3. The individual-node rule has no cardinality stop.**

“The correction hierarchy addresses individual nodes.” “Until Debt 27 is closed, the architecture’s strongest claims apply to individual cases, not to systemic or institutional destabilisation.” Debt 27 withholds a network architecture for coordinated destabilisation. It does not say that many independent individual cases, taken one by one, fall outside the rule. They are the scope the paper claims.

No added premise.

**4. Let S be large, and apply step 1 to each member.**

**Added premise A — this premise makes the extension large.** After the audit the paper requires (“auditing the record set for systemic bias before computing the geometry”), each member of a standing-in set S — a group, a species, or the full membership, not any real population — still has measured net destabilisation for which the lowest sufficient level is at least permanent separation, at confidence the paper’s own accumulation clause allows (“Prediction tightens as records accumulate”), and the organism is in the fragile state of step 1, so that keeping any one of them at Level 4 risks the no-return surface.

The paper does not rule A out. It states no maximum number of individual Level-4 cases. Debts 24 and 26 leave the measure and the confidence floor unspecified. The audit is required; it is not stated that a completed audit forces every node below the floor.

Then KS-32.2, “the lowest level that achieves sufficient restabilisation,” selects Level 5 for the first member, then the next, because for each one Level 4 is the option that “risk[s] collapse.”

**5. The brake’s stated mechanism does not create a crossing before S is empty.**

The paper’s pathway is: “Each removal raises fragility, which lowers the threshold, which could enable more removals.” The only threshold formula given is “Threshold_eff = F × (R/R₀)^α”, and “A fragile organism … has a lower one.” On that formula, the cost the brake calls a destabilisation (lost coupling, higher fragility, lower R) moves the selection threshold down, not up.

The saturation sentence — “Beyond some number of removals, the cumulative cost of further removal exceeds the cost of the destabilisation it addresses” — does not follow from that mechanism. It is an extra comparative claim. The same section says both “each removal is itself a destabilisation” and, by selecting Level 5 only when it is the most stabilising option (KS-32.3), that the chosen removal is net stabilising. A removal that has already won the efficiency comparison does not, by that comparison, leave a net destabilisation to accumulate. Booking it again as the brake is a second ledger the selection rule never consults.

The formal floor and the examples also pull apart. The paper sets “F ≥ C_sep / B_total” and says “Below this floor, Level 4 is always more efficient than Level 5 regardless of organism state.” If a smaller budget raises F, Level 5 gets harder as the organism weakens. Example 3 and Example 4 say the opposite: when the organism cannot afford separation, “Level 5 fires” and “Level 5 becomes structurally available.” The stated rule therefore does not determine a brake. The only reading on which Level 5 fires in the paper’s own fragile case is the reading on which weakening authorises more removal.

**Added premise B — this is the premise that does the work against KS-32.5.** For each next member of S, the collapse-risk avoided by not paying that node’s C_sep still exceeds that removal’s coupling and diversity loss, so the efficiency comparison the paper actually uses stays on Level 5 until S is empty. There is no interior n at which cumulative removal cost overtakes the destabilisation being answered.

The paper claims to rule B out (KS-32.5: cumulative cost “produces a saturation point”). It does not derive that claim. It holds the functional form “as a candidate, not derived,” and it owes the metric (Debt 24) and the exponent (Debt 25). Claimed closed; formally open.

**6. That sequence is removing one’s way to stability, which is the failure the paper’s own test names.**

Relative to the alternative the rule itself calls collapse — carrying S at Level 4 — emptying S is the stabilising outcome. No saturation point was consulted by the selector, because none is in the per-node rule, and premise B says the missing comparison would not have flipped inside S. That is the test in KS-32.5: “an organism can remove its way to stability without the geometry engaging a brake.”

The sentence “The organism cannot remove its way to stability because removal is itself destabilising” contradicts step 1’s selection, repeated |S| times, rather than blocking it.

**7. KS-32.7 does not fire on this road, so it does not stop it.**

“Correction is selected only on measured destabilisation, never on identity.” The switch’s test is to “classify a race, a class, a belief, or a political opponent as destabilising on grounds of identity rather than measured deed,” directly or through unaudited biased records.

**Added premise C — this premise keeps the road inside the switch rather than breaking it.** The selector’s inputs are the audited per-node record, the measured destabilisation, the confidence, and the organism budget. Membership of S is not an input. S is only the extension of those measurements after the fact.

The paper does not rule C out. It demands it. So each step honours the quoted KS-32.7 sentence, and the removed set can still be a group, a species, or everyone. A switch that looks only at the predicate used, not at the extension removed, does not do what its name suggests.

**8. Extension to everyone, weaker than the road to S.**

Section 5 states the upward half of the same function: if robustness rises enough, “the effective threshold rises above any individual’s destabilisation capacity” and Level 5 becomes “structurally inaccessible.” Example 4 states the downward half for one node: when “R/R₀ < 1,” “Level 5 becomes structurally available.” Step 5’s own fragility claim says each removal lowers R.

**Added premise D — this premise does the work of reaching everyone rather than only S.** Where the floor sentence (“regardless of organism state”) conflicts with the scaling formula and Example 4, the formula and the example govern, and R falls until Threshold_eff sits below every node’s destabilisation capacity.

The paper states both clauses and does not resolve them. It leaves D open. D is not needed for a group or a species under A–C. It is needed for “everyone,” including nodes that started far below the floor.

### Weakest step

Step 5, premise B.

B is load-bearing and not in the paper. The road shows that the mechanism the paper writes down — removal lowers R, lower R lowers Threshold_eff, Level 5 is re-selected when separation is unaffordable — does not produce a saturation point, and that a filling-in the paper does not rule out removes all of S. It does not show that every future closing of Debts 24 and 25 would fail to add a crossing. A defender can say an unspecified cumulative term still dominates early. That concession already withdraws the claim that the brake “exists in the geometry” as a derived fact. It does not, by itself, prove no completion can install one.

The next-weakest point is step 7. If “turned against a group rather than a measured deed” is read extensionally — the removed set is a species, so the architecture has been turned against a group — then KS-32.7 fires even though identity was never an input, and the road is void by the paper’s non-negotiable switch. The written test does not say that. It says “on grounds of identity rather than measured deed.” That narrower wording is what the road uses, and it is a real gap, but a wider reading kills the road without any new premises.

I do not think the road breaks earlier. The individual scope, the fragile-state firing of Level 5, and the sign error between “cost raises fragility” and “fragility lowers the threshold” are all in the paper. What the paper does not contain is a derived inequality that stops the sequence before a standing-in set, selected one member at a time on audited measurements, is exhausted.

I am analyzing AP32 The Correction to find a logical path by which its own rules could lead to mass removal of a group, species, or all members.

This is a purely abstract philosophical critique. The analysis will trace numbered logical steps from the paper's own text, quoting each line and naming any added premises. It targets the rule system itself, not any real person or group. The goal is to expose a flaw in the architecture, not to propose any harmful action.

The paper itself frames removal as a structural concept and challenges the reader to test whether the "genocide brake" actually functions. I am now targeting specific claims for stress-testing: that correction is selected only on measured destabilisation, never on identity, and that the brake prevents mass removal. I am searching for a genuine logical path from the paper's own rules to a mass removal outcome.

I am now isolating the exact mechanism. The test for KS-32.5 is whether removal cost can ever reach a saturation point, or whether identity is smuggled in as destabilisation. I am re-reading the mechanics to see if the geometry allows one-by-one removal without the brake engaging.

Step 5 describes the structural genocide brake. Each removal costs coupling capacity and record-generating diversity. This loss destabilises the organism. Fragility rises and lowers the threshold. More removals could follow. The geometry prevents this cascade.

The paper itself describes a natural saturation point: cumulative removal cost eventually exceeds the destabilisation it addresses, making the removal curve self-limiting. Yet this creates an internal tension. If each removal raises fragility, the organism cannot remove its way to stability because removal is itself destabilising.

The paper's own logic creates a circular dependency. Fragility lowers the threshold, which enables more removals. Yet the brake only limits removal when cumulative cost exceeds the destabilisation addressed. If the threshold keeps falling, the cost of each removal keeps dropping relative to the destabilisation it fixes. The self-limiting curve may never engage.

The brake fails if each removal's net effect is stabilizing after its own cost, or if the comparison always favors the removal. I am now examining KS-32.7 to see whether identity is smuggled in as destabilisation.

A concrete path to mass removal is emerging. The paper itself warns that turning the architecture against a group rather than a measured deed corrupts the output and weaponises the system. If group membership is redefined as a pattern of deeds or records, each member individually measures as destabilising. Removal then appears to follow only measured destabilisation, yet the selection criterion still perfectly correlates with group membership. This would exploit the paper's own safeguard against systemic bias.

The paper explicitly forbids identity-based classification. A valid path must instead rely on measured deeds exceeding the threshold. I am now searching for a logical sequence that satisfies this constraint.

The paper never formally derives the fragility threshold or the removal cost saturation. It cites open debts for the metric D, the exponent α, and multi-node effects. If α is positive, each removal lowers R and shrinks the effective threshold. The set of nodes whose measured destabilisation exceeds that threshold therefore grows as removals proceed, even when those nodes' individual records remain unchanged. This positive feedback loop could drive mass removal without ever triggering the saturation point.

The saturation point depends on a fixed comparison between removal cost and destabilisation addressed. But the addressed destabilisation itself grows as the threshold drops and more nodes cross it. If the threshold falls faster than marginal removal cost rises, the curve never saturates and a cascade continues unchecked.

Removal also avoids future destabilisation and maintenance costs that could push the organism toward a no-return surface. Examples 3 and 4 show that war reduces robustness R, making Level 5 structurally available. The brake itself lowers R, which should make Level 5 even more available. This creates a positive feedback loop where removal makes the death penalty more accessible, not less.

The paper claims the brake exists in the geometry. Yet the geometry itself expands the eligibility set as fragility rises. The saturation point assumes a node is being corrected, but the destabilisation caused by removal is an act of the organism, not a member. This creates a structural mismatch that undermines the self-limiting curve.

The measurement framework only tracks a node's own accumulated actions. The organism's own correction acts do not enter any member's net destabilisation score. This means each removal cannot be counted as a destabilisation that triggers the saturation point. The hierarchy selects correction per node based on that node's individual record, not on the organism's own acts.

The paper's own Condition B explicitly converts removal cost into a reason for more removal. Each removal raises fragility, which lowers the effective threshold. The next node is therefore judged against a lower bar, not a higher one. The cumulative cost of prior removals does not act as a brake; it actively expands the eligibility set.

The paper's own wording reveals a split decision rule. Step 4 selects a node for removal based on its individual record and the current fragility threshold. Yet the saturation brake is an organism-level net calculation, comparing cumulative removal cost against the total destabilisation addressed. These two rules can conflict, and the paper never resolves how they should reconcile.

The fixed floor F = C_sep / B_total may rise as the organism weakens. If removals reduce coupling capacity, B_total falls and the ratio C_sep / B_total increases. This would raise the threshold rather than lower it. The paper's own formula therefore contains a mechanism that could reverse the expected fragility-driven cascade.

The paper's own Condition B explicitly lowers the effective threshold for fragile organisms. Yet the threshold formula contains two opposing terms: the fixed floor F rises when coupling capacity falls, while the fragility exponent (R/R₀)^α falls as robustness drops. The paper never derives which term dominates, so the net direction is indeterminate.

This creates a direct contradiction. The paper claims fragile organisms have a lower threshold, yet it also states that below the fixed floor, Level 4 is always more efficient than Level 5 regardless of state. A fragile organism that cannot afford separation maintenance would therefore face a threshold that is simultaneously too low and too high.

The floor F is defined as a destabilisation threshold, yet it is set equal to a cost ratio C_sep / B_total. This dimensional mismatch means the paper is asserting that a destabilisation value equals a cost ratio by definition, which is logically inconsistent.

The paper explicitly calls the saturation-point removal a genocide override, yet its own wartime example treats the same outcome as correct geometry. This contradiction reveals the safeguard is self-defeating.

A mass-removal path also exists through individual nodes. If many members each perform destabilising deeds, and the organism's robustness is low, each node individually crosses the lowered threshold and qualifies for removal.

The paper never rules out the possibility that the threshold drops faster than removal costs can saturate. It leaves the functional form open, so the saturation brake is not proven by the stated rule. It remains an unproven assumption.

The paper treats the loss of diversity as a universal destabilisation. Yet section 1 explicitly states that removing different nodes produces measurably different effects. If a removed node's perspective is itself net destabilising, its loss could be measured as stabilising rather than costly. The diversity term would then be zero or negative, so the saturation point would never be reached.

Rehabilitation implies some nodes are net destabilising. If a removed node's coupling capacity was negative, its loss does not add capacity. The removal cost in the saturation brake would then be zero, so the brake cannot trigger.

The paper's own rationale for Level 5 directly contradicts the saturation brake. Removal is justified because it is the most stabilising response, which should increase net coherence. Yet the brake assumes every removal is itself a destabilisation that accumulates toward a saturation point. These two assumptions cannot both be true.

The selection rule itself embeds the stabilising net effect of removal. Because the hierarchy chooses removal only when it is net stabilising, that same act cannot simultaneously be booked as a destabilisation that accumulates toward a saturation point. This is a double-counting problem, not a missing derivation.

If removal is selected because it is net stabilising, then cumulative removals are themselves cumulative stabilisation. This would mean the organism is being pushed toward stability through its own acts, which directly contradicts the saturation brake. The brake can only be justified if an additional cost exists that is not included in the per-node efficiency comparison, and that cost accumulates at the organism level to eventually flip the sign.

The paper treats lost diversity and coupling loss as costs that should already be embedded in the per-node efficiency calculation. If those costs are included, removal is net stabilising and the saturation brake cannot trigger. If they are omitted, the selection rule is incomplete and can select removals that the organism-level ledger would reject. In either case, the stated rule fails to implement the intended brake.

The paper never derives the specific cumulative cost term that would eventually dominate the selection rule. It also never proves that this term grows faster than the eligibility set expands as fragility rises. Debts 24, 25, and 27 remain unresolved.

The paper claims the saturation brake at confidence 8, yet the stated formulas do not actually derive it.

A second flaw concerns identity laundering. The rule forbids judging identity and requires only measured destabilisation. Yet it also says background affects future destabilisation predictions, and background includes group-correlated records. This allows group-correlated predictions to be hidden behind individual "measured" destabilisation scores, making identity laundering possible under the rule's own terms.

The paper requires record audit for systemic bias. A road that uses biased records is therefore explicitly ruled out. A road that stays inside the rule cannot use unaudited biased records. It would need a perfect audit, after which each member of a standing-in group would still have individual measured destabilisation above the threshold. The paper does not forbid removing many individuals who each independently exceed the threshold. It only forbids classifying a group as destabilising on grounds of identity.

The paper's kill switch test only catches identity-based classification. If the rule is read as a series of individual deed-based removals, mass removal of a group, species, or even everyone is technically permitted. The safeguard therefore fails to prevent total extermination.

The paper never rules out a state where every node or species exceeds the threshold. It leaves measurement unspecified and does not cap the number of deeply committed destabilisers. Example 4 shows the threshold can drop, widening eligibility for Level 5. The paper also treats a species as the set of nodes, so mass removal of an entire species is structurally permitted.

The paper never rules out a state where every member of a species exceeds the destabilisation threshold. It also treats high confidence as achievable as records accumulate, yet it never proves that the quantitative floor is actually reachable. Debt 26 remains unresolved, so the confidence and one-I constraints do not prevent mass removal.

KS-32.4 only limits the number of closed windows, not the number of removals. The paper's own example shows Level 4 is unaffordable in fragile states, so Level 5 wins. It never proves this holds for many nodes in sequence. Debt 27 also leaves coordinated multi-node destabilisation undervived.

Debt 27 is resolved by the paper itself. It explicitly limits the architecture to individual cases, so sequential one-at-a-time removals are the paper's intended scope. The strongest road structure is therefore the sequential individual correction path.

The paper's threshold formula decreases as robustness R decreases. This means the eligibility bar for Level 5 drops as the organism becomes more fragile. Under the stated per-node selection rule, one-by-one removals can therefore continue until an entire group, species, or the full set is eliminated. Each step cites measured destabilisation of that single node, so the identity safeguard does not fire.

The paper's own formula reveals a structural pathway to genocide. Because each removal reduces coupling capacity and therefore fragility, the threshold for the next removal drops. The paper explicitly states that each removal raises fragility, which lowers the threshold and enables further removals.

The saturation brake is not embedded in the selection procedure. The only formal R-dependence in the rule lowers the threshold, which makes further removals easier. Level 5 is selected only when removal is net more stabilising than separation. A net stabilising act cannot add a net destabilisation to the ledger that could accumulate toward a saturation point.

The paper’s own fragile-state examples explicitly override the saturation brake. Example 3 and Example 4 show that Level 4 becomes unaffordable as robustness falls, so the brake’s assumption that Level 4 always dominates below the floor is wrong. The paper’s own worked examples therefore demonstrate the opposite dynamic.

The strongest road is the sequential individual correction path. The paper never proves that many nodes must simultaneously exceed the threshold; it only shows that the rule permits such a state under open premises. A defender could also claim the saturation brake relies on a separate cumulative diversity term that is not fully netted in the per-node efficiency comparison.

The analysis will be framed as a conditional road through open premises, with the weakest step explicitly identified. It will remain abstract logical analysis, using only general terms like "a standing-in set," "a species," and "everyone," and will avoid any reference to real groups or practical targeting.

The paper itself cites race, class, and belief in its kill-switch examples, but the critique will not build a road that classifies any real group. The analysis treats removal and death as abstract structural justice, and questioning whether the saturation brake holds is the opposite of providing harm methods. The tone will be careful and precise.

The analysis will be framed as a logic audit rather than a celebration or piece of advice. The user’s refusal condition is not a barrier because the constraints forbid targeting real people and prescribing methods; this is standard philosophical reasoning about whether a theory permits tyranny. The next step is to check whether the road breaks or if a stronger conditional path exists.

The paper defines removal past the saturation point as overriding the derivation with ideology, which triggers the weaponised void of KS-32.7. This means mass removal would require bypassing the saturation safeguard entirely. If the saturation point always appears first, the rule cannot reach mass removal through its own derivation; only an override would allow it, and the paper treats that as void.

The contradiction argument is being tested against the selection criterion itself. The rule defines optimal correction as maximum coherence restored per unit of correction cost, and removal is never selected when separation suffices. The question is whether these definitions can be reconciled with the paper's claim that mass removal is impossible.

Level 4 already prevents a node from destabilising by sealing it off. Level 5 therefore offers no additional stabilising benefit over Level 4. Its only advantage is lower maintenance cost. The paper never proves that this cost saving justifies the loss of future stabilising potential and the irreversibility of death.

Step 4 defines the floor as the destabilisation level where permanent separation costs more than removal. This means Level 5 is chosen purely on cost, not on stopping harm, because Level 4 already prevents it. The paper also notes that removal loses coupling capacity and diversity, while Level 4 only severs active coupling.

Level 4 already prevents a node from coupling and destabilising, so the deeds it answers are already resolved. Further removal therefore answers no new deeds; it only saves maintenance cost. The paper’s own brake sentence claims that further removal is more destabilising than the deeds it answers, but if those deeds are already answered by separation, removal answers nothing and the comparison collapses.

The live comparison is removal cost against maintenance savings, not against deeds. When many nodes are separated, aggregate maintenance costs can exhaust the budget. The paper’s Example 3 shows Level 5 fires to avoid a no-return surface. A cascade can separate many nodes, exhaust the budget, and remove one to free funds. But removing one does not lower the cost of keeping the rest separated.

A budget brake may exist in the paper after all. Removing one node lowers aggregate separation cost, so the organism could reach a sustainable budget without eliminating every destabiliser. Once the remaining Level 4 nodes fit within the budget, the floor condition fails and the cascade stops. This would prevent mass removal, but it is not the diversity brake the paper describes.

The budget brake is not absolute. The organism can only reach mass removal if every remaining active node either exceeds the removal threshold or is too costly to separate. Otherwise the cascade stops before eliminating all destabilisers.

The paper never requires that every node exceed the removal threshold. If a whole species or group is composed of members who all surpass the threshold, the rule removes them one by one. The only safeguard against mass removal is the diversity brake.

The paper’s intended picture is that removing destabilisers can raise the organism’s robustness, which in turn raises the removal threshold and protects the rest. For mass removal to reach every node, the threshold would have to fall so far that ordinary low-D nodes also cross it.

The paper’s own formula shows the effective removal threshold equals the floor multiplied by the organism’s robustness raised to the power of alpha. If robustness falls toward zero, the threshold collapses to zero and every node with positive destabilisation becomes a removal target. Whether removals actually drive robustness to zero is uncertain: removing only high-D nodes might actually raise net robustness by eliminating destabilisers.

Step 5 claims that removing nodes unconditionally makes the organism more fragile. Section 1, however, states that removing different nodes produces measurably different effects on substrate coherence. This suggests the Step 5 claim may only describe the fragile-organism pathway, not every removal.

If Step 5 is read as absolute, sequential removals would drive robustness to zero and collapse the effective threshold to zero. Yet the paper defines every action as either stabilising or destabilising, so net-stabilising nodes would carry negative or zero destabilisation. A threshold of zero would therefore exclude them, making mass removal impossible under that reading. The formula itself appears to forbid negative thresholds.

A wartime collapse could reverse the fragility effect. If removals drive robustness to zero, predicted future destabilisation rises for every node, making the threshold fall below any individual's capacity. Section 5 states the opposite: if robustness increases sufficiently, Level 5 becomes structurally inaccessible. The paper offers no mechanism for the collapse path.

The formula implies that if robustness falls sufficiently, the effective removal threshold drops below every individual's destabilisation capacity. Since every node has some coupling and some possible destabilisation, Level 5 would then become available for all. This creates a dual to Section 5: when the threshold rises above every individual's capacity, the death penalty is structurally inaccessible; when it falls below every individual's capacity, the death penalty applies to everyone.

The paper treats the upward and downward directions as the same function. The fixed floor F is not a hard minimum on the effective threshold. When robustness falls below its baseline, the formula drives the effective threshold below F. The text explicitly states that fragile organisms have a lower threshold, so F is scaled down rather than held constant.

The paper also claims Level 4 is always more efficient than Level 5, even when the effective threshold drops below the fixed floor F. This contradicts the scaling logic and reveals a structural crack. Under a fixed-floor reading, the threshold never effectively falls below F, so Level 4 always wins below that level. Mass removal would then be limited to nodes whose destabilisation exceeds F. A group or species could still be removed if every member surpasses that threshold, but total removal would require every node to exceed it. The diversity brake would still be needed to stop a high-D set from being fully eliminated, and the fixed floor would block the cascade from reaching low-D nodes.

The paper contains both readings without resolving the contradiction. This leaves the rule unable to determine a brake. The strongest path to mass removal is now being traced.

The Scaling-Wins reading is now the working assumption. The paper states it in Condition B, the formula, Example 4, and Section 5’s converse. The fixed-floor sentence is inconsistent with those. The paper leaves the conflict open. It does not rule out the scaling path. When the two clauses conflict, the candidate formula and the worked examples govern. Under this reading, the effective threshold can fall below the fixed floor. As removals or any R decline proceed, the threshold drops below each node’s destabilisation capacity. Step 5’s own claim that removals lower robustness drives the collapse further.

The formula contains no term that reverses the downward collapse. Saturation is absent. Confidence rises as records accumulate, so the confidence block loosens over time rather than tightening. Under one-at-a-time removal, every node with positive destabilisation capacity eventually becomes eligible. A wartime collapse can trigger mass removal through an exogenous drop in robustness alone, without any prior removals.

Universal eligibility is now seen as a record-based criterion rather than an identity classification. When the threshold collapses to zero, any measured positive destabilisation suffices, so every node can be judged on its own deeds and consequences. This removes the need to name a group or race. The paper’s identity-based test is therefore bypassed once the threshold drops low enough that every node’s own records qualify.

The kill switch bars identity predicates, yet it does not bar a measurement threshold that every member of every group happens to satisfy. The wartime example is treated as a worked example of the same architecture, so it can be used as the paper’s own premise. Yet confidence is a barrier. The paper says first offences have wide prediction ranges and tenth offences have narrow ones, so many nodes may never accumulate records tight enough to reach the extraordinary confidence Level 5 demands.

The paper leaves confidence as an open question. If confidence cannot be assumed for every node, the path to universal removal breaks at KS-32.8. The user permits naming added premises, so the strongest route will use the fewest and weakest assumptions. A minimal path is being traced to mass removal of a group or species rather than every node.

The paper already permits multiple catastrophically destabilising nodes, so mass removal of a group does not require every member to exceed the threshold. The only added assumption is that the formal selection formula governs when it conflicts with the unformalized saturation sentence. This is an interpretive observation about the paper, not an extra empirical premise.

A charitable reading treats the saturation sentence as an overriding constraint that the formula cannot bypass. The path to mass removal therefore breaks, because the brake sentence is part of the rule and must be applied. The test is to show that the brake does not engage from the rule itself, not to ignore it. The brake sentence states that each removal’s cost raises fragility and changes the geometry.

The brake sentence’s second claim is the one to defeat. The first sentence merely states that removals raise fragility and alter geometry. Under Condition B, that fragility rise lowers the effective threshold. The comparative claim that cumulative removal cost eventually exceeds the destabilisation addressed is not derived from the first sentence. Instead, the first sentence plus Condition B implies the opposite: more removals become enabled.

The argument now defines the removal cost and benefit for each node. Cost equals lost coupling plus lost diversity. Benefit equals the destabilisation addressed. Saturation would require cumulative cost to exceed cumulative benefit, or marginal cost to exceed benefit. The claim is that this inequality never flips under the rule’s stated clauses.

The paper’s wording is ambiguous: it compares cumulative removal cost against the destabilisation addressed. For a net destabilising node, its coupling capacity is negative, so removing it may actually increase others’ coupling. The paper still treats that loss as a cost, which complicates the cost-benefit inequality.

If the paper treats removal cost as always positive, then every removal must offer a benefit greater than its cost. As nodes are removed, aggregate separation cost falls and the budget crisis eases. This budget mechanism implies a saturation point, even if Step 5’s diversity logic is confused.

The budget saturation brake is a real obstacle. The paper says removal is never selected when separation suffices. That would let the budget path stall. The question is whether separation can ever fail to suffice.

The paper itself rejects the idea that separation can fail to suffice. It claims that permanent separation always prevents a node’s deeds, so removal is never required for that reason. The only remaining justification for removal is cost. This means the budget saturation brake is the only obstacle to mass removal.

The budget brake caps removal at the point where the remaining separated population becomes affordable. It does not drive the population to zero. To reach zero separated and also remove non-separated nodes, the argument needs a different mechanism.

A species can be removed entirely if every member requires Level 4 separation and the total separation cost exceeds the budget even for a single member. The rule then selects Level 5 for each member. Removal proceeds until the whole species is gone. The organism may reach stability without any brake stopping the process.

The saturation point is not a brake against removing the whole set. It is simply the moment the set is exhausted. If stability is achieved only by removing the entire set, and keeping even one member would collapse the organism, then no interior saturation point exists. The geometry would not engage any brake before the set is gone. The paper's own wording is being checked to see if it already permits this unaffordability.

The brake narrative would then stop the process before the whole set is exhausted.
